title: Practical ABAP: values, expressions, and failure paths
intro: Use these worked scenarios after the basic language questions. They test the consequences of parameter passing, aliasing, partial updates, and failure handling rather than syntax recall alone. Modern additions require a supporting target release and language version; examples are teaching scenarios, not executed SAP evidence.

sources.title: SAP: Sharing between dynamic data objects
SAP: LOOP AT itab, GROUP BY

questions.question: What changes when a method receives a CHANGING parameter by value instead of by reference?
questions.answer: By reference, the method works on the caller's data directly. With VALUE on a CHANGING parameter, it works on a local value and copies it back when the method finishes normally. If an exception leaves the method, that normal copy-back does not happen. This can protect the caller's value, but it does not roll back database writes or changes to shared objects.
questions.detail:
Start with a plain integer containing 10. A method changes its CHANGING parameter to 20 and then raises an exception that leaves the method. With reference passing, the caller can already see 20. With value passing, the caller retains 10 because the local result was not copied back. On normal completion, both forms can return the changed value.

That difference is important when changing an existing method signature. Tests must cover both successful completion and escaping exceptions. If the value contains an object reference, changing the referenced object is a separate effect: the copy still points to that object. VALUE is not a general undo mechanism for everything the method does.
questions.pitfall: Pass-by-value is not a transaction rollback and does not clone objects behind reference parameters.
followups: How would this change with an object reference parameter?
Can an IMPORTING reference variable still expose a mutable object?
signals: Separates input/output direction from value/reference passing
Explains when a local value is copied back
Identifies effects on the database and shared objects
questions.evidence: A small method-call test showing caller values after normal return and exception.

references.title: SAP: Pass by value
references.note: Formal parameters are local copies; parameter direction controls transfer.

questions.question: A copied structure contains a string, a nested table, and an object reference. Is it an independent snapshot?
questions.answer: Not completely. The copied string and nested internal table behave as independent values when changed. A copied object reference still points to the same object. Changing that object through either structure can therefore affect what the other sees. For a true snapshot, I decide how to handle every mutable referenced object instead of assuming ordinary assignment clones it.
questions.detail:
Suppose ls_request contains a note, an item table and a reference to a pricing object. I copy it to keep a before-change version. Editing the copied note or item values does not change the original value components. But calling a setter on the copied pricing reference changes the same pricing object used by the original structure.

If the snapshot must preserve the old price, I store the calculated price as a value, use an immutable object or implement a deliberate copy of the required object state. A full clone needs rules for shared identities and cycles. Runtime memory-sharing optimizations do not change these value-versus-reference rules; a deep ABAP type is not automatically a deep object clone.
questions.pitfall: A deep ABAP type is not a promise that ordinary assignment recursively clones the entire object graph.
followups: Which components need copying for an audit snapshot?
How would you test sharing without inspecting memory addresses?
signals: Separates copied values from copied references
Explains why both references still point to one object
Defines what a snapshot must preserve
questions.evidence: Mutation tests for a copied string, nested row, and referenced object's attribute.

references.title: SAP: Sharing between dynamic data objects
references.note: Distinguishes copying reference values from internal sharing of strings and tables.

questions.question: A large temporary internal table is no longer needed. When would you choose CLEAR or FREE?
questions.answer: For an internal table without a header line, CLEAR and FREE both remove the rows. CLEAR keeps the initial memory allocation available; FREE releases that allocation too. I use CLEAR when I expect to refill the table soon, and FREE when it is finished for now. Neither removes the variable declaration or guarantees that the operating system immediately shows lower process memory.
questions.detail:
A package loop fills a small work table, processes it and starts the next package. CLEAR is often a sensible reset because the table will be used again. Repeatedly freeing and allocating it may add unnecessary work. After a one-off large reconciliation, FREE may be appropriate when the table will no longer be needed.

I distinguish memory used by current rows from memory retained for future use, and measure in the relevant ABAP session. CLEAR does not promise to retain every byte the table ever needed. FREE also does not destroy an object that another reference still reaches. A single process-memory number cannot explain all of those separate lifetimes.
questions.pitfall: Do not claim CLEAR retains every byte ever allocated, or that FREE destroys referenced objects still reachable elsewhere.
followups: What changes for an obsolete table with a header line?
Which memory measurement would verify the effect?
signals: Separates stored rows from initial memory allocation
Considers whether the table will be reused
Does not promise immediate operating-system memory reduction
questions.evidence: Debugger memory snapshots before population, CLEAR, and FREE.

references.title: SAP: CLEAR
references.note: CLEAR releases table rows but retains the initial memory requirement; FREE releases that too.

questions.question: A dynamic ASSIGN fails, but IS ASSIGNED is still true. How can the program update the wrong field?
questions.answer: The field symbol may still point to the previous successful target after a failed dynamic ASSIGN. IS ASSIGNED only says it points somewhere; it does not prove the latest lookup worked. I check the ASSIGN result immediately. Where supported, ELSE UNASSIGN makes failure clear. Otherwise I unassign before the lookup and handle failure before writing through the field symbol.
questions.detail:
A generic mapper first assigns component PRICE and writes an amount. It then tries the misspelled component PRCIE using the same field symbol. If that lookup fails but the old assignment remains, checking only IS ASSIGNED can allow the next write to change PRICE again. The program has updated a real field, but the wrong one.

I test the sequence of one successful lookup followed by one failed lookup. An isolated failure test can miss the stale assignment. The mapper should reject the unknown component or follow a clearly defined skip rule, and it must not write through the old alias. I verify release support before using ELSE UNASSIGN syntax.
questions.pitfall: An assigned field symbol is not evidence that the most recent dynamic ASSIGN succeeded.
followups: How would you fix this on a release without ELSE UNASSIGN?
Why can a test containing only the invalid name miss the defect?
signals: Explains why the old assignment can remain
Checks the latest ASSIGN result immediately
Tests a successful lookup followed by a failure
questions.evidence: A valid-then-invalid component lookup leaves the original component unchanged.

references.title: SAP: ASSIGN, ELSE UNASSIGN
references.note: Failed assignments may preserve an earlier alias unless explicitly unassigned.

questions.question: A READ TABLE fails, yet a later IF sy-subrc = 0 takes the success branch. What do you inspect?
questions.answer: sy-subrc holds the result of the most recent statement that set it. It is not permanently attached to READ TABLE. Another statement between the read and the IF may have replaced the value. I check it immediately or save it in a named variable. Table expressions have their own exception or predicate behavior, so I do not assume they work like READ TABLE.
questions.detail:
A READ TABLE does not find an order. Before checking the result, the program uses FIND to prepare a log message, and FIND succeeds. The later IF sy-subrc = 0 now checks the FIND result, so it enters the success branch even though the order lookup failed.

I move the decision directly after the read or preserve the read result before doing other work. The regression case includes a missing order and successful log preparation, because that is the sequence that caused the bug. Not every statement changes sy-subrc, so I inspect the actual intervening statements rather than guess. A modern table expression must be handled according to its documented missing-row behavior.
questions.pitfall: Not every statement resets sy-subrc, and a table expression is not a drop-in sy-subrc-producing READ TABLE.
followups: Which exact statement last wrote sy-subrc?
Would line_exists plus a second lookup improve this case?
signals: Identifies which statement last set sy-subrc
Checks or saves the result immediately
Uses the documented result handling for each expression
questions.evidence: A regression sequence proves missing input cannot be treated as found after another operation.

references.title: SAP: SY-SUBRC
references.note: Return values belong to particular statements and can be replaced by later statements.

questions.question: An import must reject precision loss rather than silently round or truncate. Where does EXACT help?
questions.answer: EXACT checks that an assignment or calculation can produce its target value without losing information. It raises an appropriate exception when that is impossible. CONV uses normal conversion rules and is not the same check. I catch conversion failures at the input boundary and explain them to the caller. I still validate business rules, because an exact value can still be forbidden.
questions.detail:
An import receives a text value longer than the fixed-length target field. A normal conversion may discard characters, while a lossless conversion can reject that input. For a packed result with two decimals, a calculation such as one divided by three cannot be represented exactly, so EXACT is useful if rounding is prohibited.

If the business actually requires rounding, I apply the agreed rounding rule explicitly instead of treating every inexact result as invalid. I also check rules such as a positive amount, a known currency or an allowed identifier. EXACT can detect loss of technical information; it cannot decide whether a perfectly representable negative amount is acceptable for this document.
questions.pitfall: EXACT does not prove that a technically representable value is an allowed business value.
followups: Which exception family would you translate at the import boundary?
When would requiring exactness reject a legitimate business calculation?
signals: Explains the difference between CONV and EXACT
Separates conversion loss from invalid business data
Gives the caller a useful conversion error
questions.evidence: Boundary tests include fitting data, truncation, rounding, and numeric overflow.

references.title: SAP: EXACT examples
references.note: Official executable illustrations of lossless assignments and calculations.

questions.question: Two invoice totals differ by one cent although both use decimal types. How do you diagnose rounding?
questions.answer: I check where rounding happens, which rounding mode is required and the precision of intermediate values. Rounding each line and then adding can differ from adding first and rounding the total. Decimal types do not decide that business rule for me. I keep the currency context and write tests for values near the rounding boundary.
questions.detail:
Assume the agreed rule is half-up rounding to two decimals. Two positive line results are each 0.005. If each line is rounded first, each becomes 0.01 and the total is 0.02. If I add the precise values first, the sum is 0.010 and rounds to 0.01. Both calculations follow their chosen order, but only the specified order is correct for the document.

I compare the implementation with that rule, including intermediate assignments that may already round a value. I test multiple small lines, negative amounts where allowed and currency-specific requirements. Changing the display to two decimals or choosing decfloat34 does not by itself settle when or how the business wants rounding.
questions.pitfall: Choosing decfloat34 or formatting two decimals does not settle the business rounding policy.
followups: How do negative half-way values affect the selected mode?
Where is currency conversion applied relative to tax rounding?
signals: Checks precision at each calculation step
States when and how rounding occurs
Keeps the correct currency and conversion rules
questions.evidence: Worked positive/negative boundary examples with independently calculated expected totals.

references.title: SAP: Rounding function ROUND
references.note: Decimal places, precision, and explicit rounding modes are distinct choices.

questions.question: Why can replacing MOVE-CORRESPONDING with CORRESPONDING erase an existing structure field?
questions.answer: Plain CORRESPONDING builds a new result. Fields missing from the source therefore become initial in that result. MOVE-CORRESPONDING between structures keeps unmatched fields already in the target. A CORRESPONDING expression with BASE can start from existing values, but matching source fields still overwrite them, even with initial values. I choose the form based on the intended update behavior.
questions.detail:
The existing request has status Approved and a note. The incoming structure contains only a new note. MOVE-CORRESPONDING updates the note and leaves the status. Assigning a plain CORRESPONDING result replaces the whole target with a new value, so the unmatched status becomes initial. Supplying the existing structure as BASE preserves that unmatched status.

Now consider a source type that also contains status, but with a blank value. Status matches by name, so it can overwrite the BASE value with blank. BASE is not an automatic ignore-empty or PATCH rule. If an API must distinguish an omitted field from an explicitly cleared field, I define and test field-presence handling separately.
questions.pitfall: BASE preserves unmatched components; it does not mean ignore every initial source value or implement PATCH automatically.
followups: What happens when status exists but is initial in the source?
How do table BASE semantics differ from structure merging?
signals: Explains that a constructor creates a new value
Checks matching source fields that contain initial values
Separates field-name mapping from whether a field was supplied
questions.evidence: A three-case test covers absent component, initial matching component, and populated matching component.

references.title: SAP: Working with structures
references.note: Compares MOVE-CORRESPONDING with CORRESPONDING and BASE.

questions.question: Unsorted orders must be processed once per customer with their member rows. How does GROUP BY change the loop?
questions.answer: LOOP AT with GROUP BY collects rows with equal group keys even when they are not adjacent. The outer loop then runs once per group. LOOP AT GROUP can process that group's members. This avoids relying on the input being sorted for traditional control-level processing. I still define the required group and member order rather than assume grouping provides the business sort order.
questions.detail:
The input customer sequence is A, B, A. Grouping by customer creates two groups, and both A orders belong together despite being separated in the input. The group loop runs twice. Inside the A group, a member loop can calculate its total or process each of its orders.

I use an explicit group key when it makes the code easier to follow. If I request WITHOUT MEMBERS because only distinct customers are needed, I cannot later loop over the missing group members. This processing happens on an internal table in ABAP memory, not as database aggregation. If the output must be customer-sorted, I express and test that ordering instead of relying on encounter order.
questions.pitfall: Grouping an internal table is not database aggregation, and its default group order is not automatically business sort order.
followups: When would you aggregate at the database instead?
Why must a representative row not be mistaken for a group total?
signals: Explains grouping first and processing groups afterward
Groups matching rows even when separated in the input
Does not mistake one representative row for a group total
questions.evidence: An A/B/A fixture proves group membership, counts, and explicit ordering.

references.title: SAP: LOOP AT itab, GROUP BY
references.note: Grouping and group iteration are separate phases; prior sorting is not required.

questions.question: A FILTER expression is proposed for a standard table with an empty primary key. Is that enough?
questions.answer: An empty primary key alone is not enough for the basic FILTER form. It needs a suitable sorted or hashed key. A standard table can work if it has a suitable secondary key selected with USING KEY. The condition must also follow the chosen key rules. For an arbitrary condition, a FOR expression or a normal loop may be clearer.
questions.detail:
A standard table keeps orders in arrival order but also has a sorted secondary key starting with customer. A key-based FILTER can use that secondary key to select a customer according to the supported predicate rules. The table does not need to lose its arrival-order use just to gain another access path.

A condition combining unrelated fields with a complex OR is a different problem. I do not force it into FILTER just because the syntax looks shorter. A straightforward loop or suitable FOR expression can express the intended rule more clearly. I check the actual key definition and target-release syntax, then measure if performance matters; the keyword alone does not prove a faster implementation.
questions.pitfall: FILTER is not a general-purpose synonym for every WHERE expression supported by LOOP or FOR.
followups: What must a hashed-key predicate provide?
Would adding a secondary key be worthwhile for a single filtering pass?
signals: Names the sorted or hashed key needed
Checks which conditions that key supports
Compares faster reads with key-maintenance cost
questions.evidence: Target-release syntax check plus equivalence tests against an explicit loop.

references.title: SAP: FILTER, basic form
references.note: Defines sorted/hash key requirements and supported predicate forms.

questions.question: A REDUCE expression calculates a maximum, but all-negative input returns zero. What went wrong?
questions.answer: The initial accumulator value is wrong for this input. Starting a maximum at zero makes zero a candidate, even if every real value is negative. I start from a valid member or represent no result explicitly. I also define what empty input means. REDUCE makes the loop concise, but it does not choose the correct starting value or numeric type for me.
questions.detail:
For values -8 and -3, the maximum is -3. An accumulator initialized to zero stays at zero because neither input is larger. The result looks like a valid number but does not occur in the input and is not its maximum. Initializing from a valid first member avoids that invented candidate.

An empty table needs a separate decision: perhaps return an optional result, or raise a meaningful exception if at least one value is required. I test empty, all-negative, mixed and single-value inputs. I also check intermediate type limits and rounding. A reviewer should be able to see initialization, comparison and update clearly; if the expression hides them, I use a named step or loop.
questions.pitfall: REDUCE does not supply mathematically correct initial values or empty-set semantics on the developer's behalf.
followups: How would you represent maximum of an empty set?
Can a narrow accumulator overflow before assignment to a wider result?
signals: Chooses a valid starting accumulator value
Defines the result for empty input
Checks types used during calculation
questions.evidence: Tests cover empty, one row, all-negative values, mixed signs, and overflow limits.

references.title: SAP: Table reductions, structured result
references.note: Shows explicit initialization and iterative accumulator updates.

questions.question: A report accepts a filter value and a sort-column name. Is escaping quotes sufficient for safe SQL?
questions.answer: No. A filter value and a column name are different kinds of input. I pass values through host variables in static ABAP SQL where possible. For a configurable column or dynamic clause, I map approved choices to known SQL elements and reject anything else. Escaping quotes in a value does not make arbitrary SQL text safe or authorized.
questions.detail:
A customer name containing an apostrophe should be treated as a value, not assembled into executable SQL text. A requested sort option is different: I map an accepted choice such as newest to a known timestamp column and direction. I do not accept any string and insert it as ORDER BY syntax.

Mandatory authorization restrictions are built separately from optional user filters. The user must not be able to remove them by changing a filter or sort parameter. I test unknown columns, invalid directions and inputs containing SQL-like text, as well as ordinary names. Safe quoting protects one kind of value; it does not approve table names, operators, whole conditions or access to restricted data.
questions.pitfall: Input that is safely quoted as a literal is not therefore safe as SQL syntax or an authorized data access.
followups: How would you test an input that is valid syntax but unauthorized?
Which parts of the SQL shape can remain completely static?
signals: Separates data values from SQL names and syntax
Maps choices to explicitly allowed SQL elements
Keeps mandatory authorization conditions in place
questions.evidence: Negative tests for quoted values, forbidden columns, injected operators, and unauthorized records.

references.title: SAP: Prevent SQL injection
references.note: Prefer static SQL; validate and escape dynamic content using supported facilities.

questions.question: A resource release is placed only in CLEANUP. Why can it remain unreleased after success?
questions.answer: CLEANUP is not a finally block that runs after every TRY. It is used during the relevant exception propagation to an outer handler. It does not run just because normal processing reaches ENDTRY. I arrange release on success and on the required error paths. I also check who owns the resource so I do not release framework-owned locks too early.
questions.detail:
A method opens an application-owned temporary handle and processes data successfully. If release exists only in CLEANUP, reaching ENDTRY normally leaves that handle open. An exception caught inside the same TRY also does not make CLEANUP a universal after-CATCH step. I therefore make the successful release and exceptional release paths explicit.

I test normal completion, a locally handled exception and an exception that leaves for an outer handler. Release can fail too, so I handle that without hiding the original error or letting an exception escape CLEANUP. The same reasoning applies to lock ownership: cleanup must respect the intended lifetime, not remove a framework lock while the business transaction still needs it.
questions.pitfall: Do not assume CLEANUP automatically runs after a CATCH in the same TRY, or release framework-owned locks prematurely.
followups: What changes when the exception is caught inside the same TRY?
Who owns release when a caller supplied the resource?
signals: Explains why CLEANUP is not a general finally block
Tests successful and failed execution
Releases only resources owned by this code
questions.evidence: Instrumented resource tests show one correct release on every intended exit.

references.title: SAP: Exception system response
references.note: Explains stack unwinding and when CLEANUP blocks run or do not run.

questions.question: An optional limit parameter is omitted in one call and explicitly set to zero in another. How can a method distinguish them?
questions.answer: IS SUPPLIED checks whether the caller passed the parameter. IS INITIAL checks its value. Those are different: an omitted parameter and an explicit zero can both contain zero. I use presence only when omission has a defined meaning in the API. A wrapper must preserve that meaning, because forwarding its own initial variable makes the downstream parameter supplied.
questions.detail:
A helper treats an omitted limit as use the configured default, while a supplied zero means return no rows. Checking IS INITIAL cannot distinguish these calls. IS SUPPLIED can, so the helper first decides which meaning the caller requested and then applies the value rule.

A wrapper introduces another risk. If it always forwards its own optional parameter variable, the next method sees a supplied argument even when the original caller omitted it. I test the direct calls and the wrapper path, and forward conditionally or pass explicit presence information where appropriate. OPTIONAL permits omission; it does not automatically carry that omission through every later method call.
questions.pitfall: OPTIONAL does not automatically preserve absent-versus-present semantics across another method boundary.
followups: What happens when a wrapper always forwards an optional argument?
Would an explicit request structure with a presence flag be clearer?
signals: Separates omitted arguments from initial values
Checks what wrappers forward
Defines what omission means
questions.evidence: Calls with omitted, explicit zero, and positive limit produce their documented outcomes.

references.title: SAP: IS SUPPLIED
references.note: Presence of an actual argument is independent of its initial value.

questions.question: A single-line INSERT INTO TABLE hits an existing unique primary key. Does it update the existing row?
questions.answer: No. In this single-row internal-table INSERT case, a duplicate unique primary key prevents insertion and is reported through sy-subrc. The existing row is not updated. I decide whether duplicates should be rejected, merged or replaced and implement that decision explicitly. Other insertion forms and secondary-key conflicts can behave differently, so I do not generalize this return-code rule.
questions.detail:
An import contains order 7 twice, first with amount 100 and then with amount 200. Inserting both into a hashed table with a unique order key does not replace 100 with 200 automatically. If the program ignores the failed insertion, it may silently keep the first row and hide conflicting input.

I define the import rule before coding. Identical duplicates might be acceptable, in which case I compare the relevant values. Conflicting duplicates should produce a useful error with the order and input position, unless a deliberate replacement rule exists. I check sy-subrc immediately for this operation and test both cases. Uniqueness prevents duplicate keys; it does not explain which business value should win.
questions.pitfall: Uniqueness enforcement is not a complete deduplication policy, and INSERT is not an automatic upsert.
followups: What should happen for identical versus conflicting duplicates?
Why must constructor-expression and secondary-key failures be checked separately?
signals: States the result of this single-row primary-key conflict
Defines how to handle identical and conflicting duplicates
Does not assume all insert forms fail the same way
questions.evidence: Tests distinguish new keys, identical duplicates, and conflicting duplicates without changing the original row accidentally.

references.title: SAP: Populating internal tables
references.note: Single-line insertion with duplicate unique primary key returns sy-subrc 4.

questions.question: An authorization helper returns an empty range table. Why is WHERE field IN range unsafe as the only access restriction?
questions.answer: An empty ABAP selection range means no restriction for IN. It does not mean the user is allowed no values. If an authorization lookup returns no allowed plants, I return no data or reject the request before querying. I keep mandatory access restrictions separate from optional user filters. Nonempty ranges also have inclusion and exclusion rules, not just list membership.
questions.detail:
A user has no permission for any plant. The helper returns an empty range, and a query uses WHERE plant IN that range as its only access check. The initial range does not narrow the selection, so the query can expose records the user should never see. The program must handle the no-permission result explicitly first.

I test a user with no allowed plants, one allowed plant and relevant exclusions. I also test that adding or omitting a user search filter cannot remove the mandatory restriction. An empty optional filter may correctly mean show all permitted data; an empty authorization result means no permitted data. They must not share an ambiguous representation without an explicit check.
questions.pitfall: An empty ABAP selection range is not the same as an SQL list containing zero allowed values.
followups: How do you distinguish an optional filter from mandatory authorization?
What result do you expect from a range containing only exclusions?
signals: Explains why an empty range does not restrict IN
Returns no data when there are no permissions
Separates optional search filters from required access checks
questions.evidence: A denied-user test proves zero data and zero aggregate leakage with an empty authorization result.

references.title: SAP: Comparison with selection tables
references.note: Defines inclusion/exclusion semantics and the initial selection-table case.
